title: NAB reveals 15pc plunge in new home loans
full_text:
National Australia Bank has revealed a bleak outlook for home lending after new mortgage applications crashed 15 per cent in the June quarter, mirroring a plunge in auction clearance rates.
This comes as NAB revealed concerns more business borrowers could be in distress, with loans classified as “on watch” up 8 per cent quarter on quarter, signifying the possibility of rising arrears down the track.
However, formally recognised bad debts are improving for the Melbourne-based bank, according to an update from its business and private banking arm on Thursday. The proportion of bad loans to gross loans and acceptances, the core metric used to measure credit quality, improved from 3 per cent at the end of the March quarter to 2.91 per cent at the end of June.
NAB business banking executive Andrew Auerbach told The Australian the higher level of loans on watch simply reflected “the impact of our challenging environment”.
“We’re seeing customers most affected by things like the fuel price and Middle East,” he said.
Mr Auerbach said the commercial arm had “continued to perform well in a challenging economic environment”.
“It’s pleasing to see the resilience of our business customers who continue to find opportunities to grow and innovate,” he added.
NAB’s overall loan book rose 4 per cent, with June 2026 the strongest month for the bank since the 2022 financial year. Loans hit $295bn in June in the business and private bank.
But mortgage applications for business and private bank customers were down 9 per cent in the June quarter, compared to a 15 per cent drop in home loans across all of NAB including its digital brand ubank. Mr Auerbach said NAB’s business customers had offset an otherwise gloomy outlook for property lending.
The Albanese government’s negative gearing and capital gains tax changes are thought to be accelerating a housing downturn that began when the Reserve Bank hiked interest rates.
Core support for Labor fell from 33 per cent to 30 per cent, which reflects the ALP’s lowest point since the Gillard government polled between 26 per cent and 30 per cent, Newspoll revealed a fortnight ago.
Auction clearance rates for the week ended July 26 were 53.3 per cent in Sydney, and 51.7 per cent in Melbourne according to Cotality.
Mr Auerbach also noted that changes to broker commissions had also come into effect in the second quarter. The softer loan flow as a result “could be a part” of the same phenomenon.
The economy was nonetheless showing “resilience”, with business confidence on the up. “Our customers are very resilient and are playing the long game,” he said.
Not all states were equal for the bank – Queensland was particularly strong but Victoria was soft, although Mr Auerbach said NAB’s customers in the state were showing an interest in growth.
On Wednesday, the boss of private credit lender Metrics, Andrew Lockhart, said he expected sluggish economic growth and depressed demand for credit for the next nine to 12 months.
“I think as we then think about pent-up demand, rising rents, interest rates coming off, giving consumers the opportunity to borrow to acquire their own house again, I think that market comes back,” he said.
NAB customer deposits were up in June, to $254bn. But growth in deposits has slowed.
Morgan Stanley analyst Richard Wiles said the banking sector was facing a “shift in operating conditions”, with a weak housing market to impact performance in 2026 and 2027. In a note to clients, Mr Wiles said the changes to property related tax concessions would depress the sector. But he said some lenders would also face higher loss rates as the economy slowed.
